newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Analysts say Sweden to resist ERM pressure.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Analysts say Sweden to resist ERM pressure.

text.p: Sweden will not bow to increasing pressure from other European countries and international bankers to join Europe's monetary union as domestic politics preclude any fast move, analysts said on Monday.
Sweden was in the sportlight following Finland's decision at the weekend to link its currency, the markka, to Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).
"Clearly people are trying to pressure the Swedish government into putting the crown into the ERM but I don't think it'll budge," said economist James McKay of Paine Webber.
"(Prime Minister) Goran Persson and the Social Democrats have more pressing domestic issues ... and need to keep the support of the Swedish people."
A European Union (EU) poll found Swedes were the union's most unwilling citizens with 36 percent of those questioned saying membership in 1995 had been the wrong decision.
A common attitude was that only large companies, politicians and bureaucrats gained from membership.
"To try to link further with Europe would be dangerous on political grounds, especially with a general election due in 1998," McKay said.
"EU sentiment in Sweden over the next six months is quite important for which way Sweden will go on the EMU," said Lehman Brothers economist Keld Holm.
"There's no doubt that hostility among Swedish voters about EMU makes politicians tread water in the hope that support will increase."

Sweden's Finance Minister Erik Asbrink and Persson reiterated their stance on ERM and EMU, saying Sweden would not be swayed by another country's actions and a decision would not be taken until a party conference late 1997.
"We will not be influenced in our decision by what others do," Persson said in a Swedish radio interview. "Every party in Sweden is against EMU and therefore ERM."

Head of the European Monetary Institute (EMI) Alexandre Lamfalussy joined the growing band putting pressure on the reluctant nation, on Monday saying Sweden must join the EMU if it fulfils the Maastricht convergence criteria.

"My opinion is that a country should be in the ERM for two years before it can enter the EMU, that is also the interpretation of the majority (of countries) of the convergence criteria," Lamfalussy said after an EMU seminar.
This would imply joining the ERM before the turn of the year as the currency union is due to start January 1, 1999.
He said there was a clear risk involved in not pegging the crown in the ERM if Sweden plans to join the EMU at the start.
But Julian Callow, economist at Kleinworth Benson, said technically the Maastricht Treaty might say one thing, but in practice something else could happen.
"At the end of the day if Sweden does not want to join EMU it doesn't have to. The rest of Europe can't make Sweden join," Callow said.
Holm said this dilemma will come to the forefront more.
"Sweden and the UK have a different interpretation than the EMI. You have Sweden and Britain claiming their interpretation is currency stability, not membership of ERM.
"There's no doubt that once you've signed the (Maastricht) treaty, you're in.
"I can't see that you can force Sweden in against its will but on the other hand I don't think Sweden will want to be seen as breaking an international treaty it has already signed."
Swedish debt yields ended Monday mixed with T-bill rates slightly lower and bond yields pushed higher by foreign debt.
Dealers said Finland's widely expected decision to link the markka to ERM had little impact on the Swedish debt market.
"The Swedish stance that an ERM link is not at the agenda is also well known," said one dealer.
The crown firmed to 4.2950 to the mark from 4.3100.
